title: Grief that teaches nothing
hookLine: after his son Waldo died, Emerson wrote that grief could teach him nothing (Experience, 1844)

lines: ON A STAIR, IN A FOG.
cards: "Where do we find ourselves?" That's how Emerson opens his essay Experience.
Not with an answer, but with a fog: we wake and find ourselves on a stair, with stairs below we seem to have climbed and stairs above going up out of sight.
A little further in comes something some readers hear behind the whole essay. Emerson's young son, Waldo, had died.

And Emerson, a writer known for lifting people up, says something that can still unsettle a reader: grief had not taught him anything. This path has sat with grief before, beside Patacara on her road.

teach.h: A BEAUTIFUL ESTATE, AND NO MORE.
teach.b: First, the loss. Emerson writes that losing his son felt like losing a beautiful estate, and no more. That he cannot get it nearer to him.
Some readers find that cold. Others hear a man too stunned to make the loss into anything.
Second, the line: "I grieve that grief can teach me nothing, nor carry me one step into real nature." Notice what he's grieving. Not only his son, but that the grief opens nothing up.
No lesson, no deeper insight. Third, why that matters. People in sorrow are sometimes told that everything happens for a reason, or that this will make them stronger.
Some find comfort in that. Emerson, at least here, won't say it. There's respect in his refusal, for his son and for anyone whose grief hasn't turned into wisdom and may never.
A loss is allowed simply to be a loss. Fourth, he keeps writing. The essay doesn't end in the fog.
Page after page, he asks how to live in the days we actually have, and lands on filling the hour, living the present well. He doesn't claim the grief taught him that.

teach.h: HE KEEPS WALKING UP THE STAIR.
teach.b: He just keeps walking up the stair.
Sometimes that's all there is to do with a sorrow that makes no sense: carry it, and keep going.

how: Readers often return to this passage in Experience when grieving, finding in it permission not to turn a loss into a lesson.

games.q: what does “grief that teaches nothing” mean?
o: Emerson's honesty that his son's death brought no lesson
the idea that every sorrow hides a lesson to be learned
a sadness so brief that it leaves no mark behind

games.q: inside Emerson's Experience: tap the pairs.
p: stairs below and above, out of sight
a beautiful estate, and no more

s: Emerson writes that his grief made him wiser
he grieves that grief can teach him nothing.
the essay Experience opens with a question
Emerson ends the essay still lost in the fog
he goes on to ask how to live the days we actually have.

games.q: you're Emerson, writing an essay after the death of your young son. readers expect wisdom from you. what do you write?
o: that everything happens for a reason.
games.why: he writes: "I grieve that grief can teach me nothing, nor carry me one step into real nature." he refuses to make the loss into a lesson.

practice: If a loss comes to mind, a person, a place, a hope, let it be here without asking it to mean anything, the way you might sit beside someone without talking. If nothing comes, or if today it's too much, simply rest with your breath.
And if grief ever brings thoughts of harming yourself, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number; you don't have to carry it alone.

wordCard.voice: Grief that teaches nothing. Emerson, in Experience, after his son's death: grieving that grief could not carry him one step further. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: it taught nothing. A loss doesn't have to earn its place by teaching. See you tomorrow.
